title: Teaching
text:
I teach students to think scientifically and become increasingly independent. In research-methods and social-psychology courses, that means giving students structured opportunities to practice difficult skills, receive feedback, and then use those skills in more independent work.
I use scaffolding not to lower expectations, but to make high expectations attainable. I also want students to leave psychology courses better able to evaluate evidence they encounter outside the classroom, whether or not they continue in psychology.

title: Teaching
text:
Courses Taught

PSY 250: Research Design & Analysis I
Instructor of Record, Summer 2026
Online asynchronous
I independently developed the recorded lectures, weekly learning activities, smaller assignments, exams, detailed assignment instructions and rubrics, and grading and feedback structures for this course. I also supervised two undergraduate teaching assistants.
Students learn to design research, evaluate the strengths and limitations of different methods, write scientifically, and develop an APA-style research proposal. The semester-long proposal moves from article review and literature searching through research-question development, hypotheses and variables, an introduction outline, peer review, a method outline, a full introduction, the final proposal, and a presentation. Students receive feedback at multiple points before completing the final product.
I designed the asynchronous lectures to require active participation rather than passive video viewing. Recorded lessons include prediction questions, application prompts, example generation, and brief reasoning checks. Many are graded for completion so that students can practice before they are expected to be correct and still receive useful feedback.


PSY 317: Social Psychology Lab
Instructor of Record, Summer 2024, Fall 2024, Summer 2025, and Summer 2026
Fall 2024 included two fully in-person sections; summer offerings were online asynchronous.
PSY 317 is an upper-level social-psychology laboratory and seminar centered on replication and the replication crisis, preregistration, registered reports, questionable research practices, publication bias, open science, research design, scientific disagreement, and transparent scientific writing. Students work toward designing a preregistered social-psychology study and communicating its hypotheses, design, measures, analytic approach, and implications.
The department determines the course’s core requirements and broad assignments. Within that shared framework, I have adapted the delivery, readings, activities, pacing, scaffolding, detailed instructions, grading criteria, and feedback structure for my sections.

title: Teaching
text:
How I Teach

Build Independence Through Scaffolding
The PSY 250 research proposal is my clearest example. Students first learn to read a springboard article and search the literature, then develop a research question, hypotheses, and variables. Outlines, peer review, and a full introduction give them opportunities to use feedback before they integrate the pieces into a complete proposal and presentation.


Teach Students to Trace Claims Back to Evidence
In one activity, students locate popular articles that make claims about detox diets, identify the scientific sources those articles cite, find the original research, and compare what the evidence supports with how the claim is presented publicly. The exercise turns scientific literacy into a concrete habit: follow a claim back to its evidence before deciding what to believe.


Learn Actively
I use think-pair-share, small-group discussion, student-generated examples, and applied research-design exercises to help students practice reasoning during class. In research-team meetings, I sometimes adapt this format into “Think–Pair–Walk–and–Share,” giving students time to develop an answer with a partner while adding movement to a long discussion session.


Structure Collaboration
Group work is organized around explicit roles, milestones, peer evaluation, and clear individual responsibilities. Student feedback has also made asynchronous summer group coordination an area of continued revision: collaboration should support learning without creating unnecessary logistical barriers.


Connect Learning to Transferable Skills
Students practice critical thinking, project management, communication, teamwork, public speaking, and evidence evaluation. These skills remain useful whether or not a student continues in psychology.


Practice Reflective Improvement
I have reduced readings in PSY 317 where possible, improved pacing and scaffolding, clarified the online course structure, and continued revising embedded activities for accessibility. I am also reconsidering how group work can preserve collaborative learning in asynchronous summer courses without making coordination the main challenge.

title: Teaching
text:
Evidence of Teaching Effectiveness
Across my courses, students consistently highlight knowledge of the material, organization, critical thinking, engagement, accessibility, and detailed feedback.

“I liked how the course built up to the final replicability project instead of having us do it all at once. The smaller assignments and discussions helped me understand each part of the research process before putting everything together.”


“Even though this class was an online class over the summer I do think it was spaced out well and not overly heavy on class work. I also think it was really helpful to have each portion of the research proposal spread out over time to be able to then put it all together at the end.”

title: Teaching
text:
Feedback-Driven Revision
I use student feedback to identify what I can change without sacrificing the learning goals of a course. In PSY 317, for example, I have reduced unnecessary reading, refined pacing and scaffolding, and made the online course structure more transparent. Feedback from summer students has also led me to reconsider how group projects can preserve collaborative learning without creating unnecessary coordination barriers in an asynchronous format.
Feedback on embedded lecture activities in PSY 250 has prompted me to consider ways to make active-learning prompts easier to preview and revisit, particularly for students who find switching between video and response tasks cognitively demanding.

PhD Candidate in Applied Social and Health Psychology
Colorado State University


My research examines how health-promoting behaviors can fit into everyday life without creating unrealistic demands on people’s time, attention, or routines. I focus primarily on physical activity and sedentary behavior, using workplace and everyday settings to study when movement is feasible, how people respond differently to the same intervention, and what supports sustained behavior change.
Across this work, I am especially interested in when, for whom, and under what conditions an intervention works. My research combines laboratory experiments with mixed-methods and field studies to understand both whether an intervention is effective and whether people can realistically use it.

title: Mentoring
text:
I want research assistants to leave the lab with more than completed hours. Their experience should help them build research skills, confidence, career clarity, and increasing independence. Because students enter the lab with different goals, I begin by learning what they hope to gain from the experience and then adjust their training accordingly.
A student considering a research-intensive graduate program may move toward literature review, analysis, conference presentations, and manuscript writing. A student pursuing another career may focus more on communication, teamwork, project management, participant interaction, and scientific literacy. The goal is not to push every student toward academia, but to make the research experience useful for where they want to go.

title: Mentoring
text:
A Developmental Approach

Individualize the Mentoring Experience
I meet with students to discuss why they joined the lab, which skills they want to develop, their career interests and graduate-school plans, and how much time they expect to remain involved. Those conversations help us identify responsibilities and opportunities that fit their goals.


Build Structure First
New research assistants begin with detailed written protocols, mock sessions, research-ethics guidance, expectations for documentation and reliability, competency checks, and close feedback. Clear structure gives students a dependable basis for learning and protects the quality of the research.


Transfer Autonomy
Development begins with following a protocol accurately, then moves toward understanding why each procedure exists. With experience, students learn to troubleshoot problems, connect procedures with study design and data quality, and make increasingly independent decisions within their roles.


Create Opportunities for Leadership
Advanced roles have included research-assistant coordinator, shift coordinator, recruitment coordinator, data-quality coordinator, science-communication coordinator, project manager, peer trainer, and project-specific team leader. Students in these roles may schedule or train peers, monitor data quality, coordinate recruitment, improve workflows, or manage a defined part of a study.

title: Mentoring
section: Weekly Lab Meetings as a Research Seminar
text:
Weekly Lab Meetings as a Research Seminar
Weekly lab meetings are a major educational part of the research experience. During active studies, we review protocol deviations and recurring data-quality issues, not simply to identify mistakes but to understand how they affect research rigor. Meetings also include discussion of an assigned article, student-generated questions, small-group and full-group discussion, methods mini-lessons, applied exercises, project updates, and conversations about conferences and manuscripts.
For example, a discussion of qualitative research may include a short interview excerpt that students practice coding together, while a paper using meta-analysis can become an opportunity to explain how effect sizes are synthesized across studies.

title: Mentoring
text:
Learning the Research Lifecycle
Students enter projects at different stages, but I help them see how the pieces connect. Depending on timing and interest, they may contribute to idea development, literature review, protocol development, institutional review, recruitment, data collection, quality control, analysis, conference dissemination, or manuscript writing. Project updates and lab meetings help students understand stages they do not experience directly.
One example of this progression is Smriti Maskey, who began on my research team running study sessions and later became involved in literature review, study planning, project coordination, conference presentations, and manuscript writing. Our mentoring relationship continued after she left CSU, and she is now pursuing a PhD in Clinical Psychology at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee.

title: Mentoring
text:
Evidence of Mentoring Effectiveness
Across multiple cohorts from 2022 to 2026, research assistants consistently rated the mentoring experience highly, with an average overall mentor rating of 4.91/5.

“I learned about several steps in the research process that I wouldn’t have learned in class.”


“I have learned so much being in this lab. I felt like I was able to grow a lot personally and academically.”

Students also frequently describe gaining experience with study design, protocol administration, participant interaction, literature searching, data collection, research ethics, troubleshooting, and scientific communication.

title: Mentoring
text:
Mentoring Other Mentors
I have also shared and extended this work through an invited CSU talk, “Becoming Effective Graduate Student Mentors,” and an SPSP session on the transition from graduate student to mentor. At the Rocky Mountain Psychological Association, I presented work on undergraduate research-assistant development and a lab promotion system that creates structured paths toward leadership. I co-authored a Society of Behavioral Medicine Outlook article on contextual and impactful mentoring and contribute to mentor training and evaluation through CSU’s Graduate School and Mentor Well work.

title: Mentoring
text:
Continuing to Improve My Mentoring
Research-assistant feedback has encouraged me to provide more exposure to data analysis, results interpretation, statistics, and manuscript writing. In response, I am developing more analysis mini-lessons, data-to-figure exercises, and manuscript pathways for advanced students, while explaining earlier in training how careful data collection contributes to the final scientific product.

title: Research
text:
My research examines how health-promoting behaviors can be designed around the constraints of everyday life, including timing, task demands, individual differences, and the cognitive or practical burden of making healthier choices.
The long-term question is straightforward but scientifically demanding: How can we make healthy behavior actually work in real life? I approach this question as a theory-informed, mechanism-aware, application-driven behavioral scientist.


01


I study whether and how physical activity can be integrated into desk-based work and other everyday settings without unacceptable performance, comfort, or experience tradeoffs.



02


Average effects can conceal meaningful heterogeneity. My work asks when, for whom, and under what conditions an intervention functions as a resource, an added demand, or a neutral option.



03


Health behavior interventions need to support more than one-time choices. I am interested in low-burden intervention delivery, repeated behavior, sustained use, and downstream well-being.

title: Research
text:
Laboratory-To-Field Logic
My program deliberately moves between controlled and applied settings.

Mechanism Feasibility Field effectiveness Sustained use Refined mechanism

This iterative approach lets practical constraints become part of the science rather than a problem discovered only after an intervention leaves the laboratory.

title: Research
text:
Representative Projects


Activity-Permissive Workstations, Performance, and User Experience

Movement integration · task compatibility · user experience

This randomized laboratory study compared sitting, standing, and treadmill walking during desk-based tasks. Findings suggest that treadmill walking can be compatible with some cognitive tasks, while fine-motor interaction may feel more difficult. The broader takeaway is that task-specific compatibility is more useful than asking whether treadmill desks are globally good or bad.


Activity-Permissive Workstations and Acute Social-Evaluative Stress

Stress · psychophysiology · workstation conditions

This preregistered randomized experiment tested whether walking during an acute stressor buffered or compounded stress responses. The preregistered stress-buffering hypothesis was not supported, but walking was not associated with amplified subjective stress and was rated as enjoyable. The study highlights the importance of appropriate physiological baselines when movement itself changes cardiovascular indicators.
Status: First-author manuscript under review at Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.


Dissertation: Timing of Walking Around Acute Stress

Timing · heterogeneity · mixed methods

My dissertation asks whether it matters if a brief walking bout occurs before, during, or after an acute stressor. Current quantitative results do not support a universal stress-regulation benefit of walking timing, while qualitative accounts suggest meaningful heterogeneity in how participants experience walking as preparation, coping, distraction, added demand, or recovery support.
Status: Dissertation proposal passed August 28, 2026; expected Ph.D. completion Summer 2027.


Task-Specific Treadmill-Desk Feasibility

Everyday office tasks · qualitative and mixed-methods work

This mixed-methods line examines which everyday office tasks are compatible with treadmill walking and why. Emerging themes include task demands, ergonomics, social visibility, user control, and pace.
Status: Mixed-methods manuscript development with student mentee involvement.


Longitudinal Treadmill-Desk Field Pilot

Field pilot · daily diary · sustained use

This one-year field pilot follows sustained, self-directed treadmill-desk use among administrative staff. The study is best understood as an intensive longitudinal pilot/case study designed to inform future work on adherence, context, barriers, and person-specific use patterns.


Health Literacy and Menu Labeling

Health literacy · menu labeling · intervention heterogeneity

My published work on health literacy and menu labeling shows that health information interventions do not affect all consumers uniformly. This line is a complementary research domain and a conceptual bridge to the broader question of person-by-intervention fit.

title: Research
text:
Methodological Approach
My work uses randomized experiments, mixed methods, intensive longitudinal and daily-diary field designs, psychophysiological measurement, qualitative interviews, online survey/RCT data, and applied statistical modeling. Across methods, I prioritize feasibility, acceptability, heterogeneity, and translation.

title: Research
text:
Research Trajectory
As an independent faculty member, I plan to build a program on context-sensitive health behavior interventions that reduce the burden of healthy action by fitting movement or other health behaviors into people’s existing tasks, routines, and constraints. Future projects may include task-movement compatibility frameworks, person-by-context moderators of intervention response, and larger field studies using repeated-measures or wearable-supported designs.
